@graph.name: Delivery Windows & Transit Operations
@graph.description: Delivery windows and transit operations for long-distance moving — published as domain education only: no delivery window, spread, date, or tracking practice is published for the company, and nothing in this dataset promises one. The standard model is the delivery spread: a range of dates — commonly 7 to 21 days in van-line practice and 3 to 14 days in published mover ranges — that widens with distance and peak season, is written into the bill of lading, and ends with the driver calling 24 to 48 hours ahead. Exclusive-use and expedited models put one shipment on one truck for tighter dates at a premium. A guaranteed date is a contractual commitment, a different instrument entirely. Consolidation sets the order: route order sets delivery order, and small shipments fill around large ones. Delay factors are structural: weather, federal hours-of-service rules, traffic, and route stops. Client preparation for any window: an essentials kit kept with the client, not on the truck — clothes, toiletries, medications, documents, laptops, and first-night kitchen and bedding. Carrier updates during transit are a domain expectation in the wider market; they are recorded here as education, never as a company tracking claim. The window question is the buyer's top unanswered question on a long-distance move; the company's answer is given per move at quote time, from the client's own dates.

@graph.name: Commercial Terms & Cost Drivers
@graph.description: Commercial terms and cost drivers for long-distance moving. The company's only pricing term is the published one: one flat rate agreed in writing before the truck rolls — no meter, and no company price, fee, deposit, or discount stated anywhere in this dataset. Everything else here is domain education, researched and labeled, with the federal rules cited to the FMCSA and 49 CFR Part 375. Estimate types (domain): a binding estimate fixes the price when the inventory is unchanged, with a revised written estimate if items or services are added; a binding-not-to-exceed estimate sets a ceiling, and the customer pays less when the shipment weighs less; a non-binding estimate lets the actual weight govern, with delivery-day collection capped at 110 percent of the estimate and the balance billed within 30 days — the federal 110 percent rule. Valuation (domain, FMCSA): Full Value Protection means the mover repairs, replaces, or pays the current replacement value of a lost or damaged item, with a minimum declared value of $6 per pound of shipment weight and a written declaration required for items worth more than $100 per pound; Released Value Protection is free and caps liability at $0.60 per pound per article — $15 for a 25-pound television — and is chosen only by a signed waiver on the bill of lading. Valuation is not insurance; it is a tariff-based level of carrier liability. Cost drivers (domain): weight on certified scales, with a plus-or-minus 10 percent estimate variance an industry-standard tolerance; mileage and distance brackets, which are not linear; fuel surcharges, commonly 8 to 15 percent in published guides; accessorials — stairs per flight, elevator reservation, long carry beyond roughly 75 feet, a shuttle when the truck cannot reach the home, packing, crating, and specialty handling — published as domain ranges only, never company fees; and seasonality, with peak season May through September commonly 20 to 40 percent higher in published guides, month-end premiums, and interstate booking 6 to 8 weeks ahead.

@graph.name: Federal Rule Table — Interstate Household Goods (49 CFR Part 375)
@graph.description: The federal constants every interstate household-goods move runs under, stated once, accurately, with their sources — the rule table the long-distance dataset is built on (FMCSA, "Your Rights and Responsibilities When You Move", 49 CFR Part 375 Appendix A, reproduced at fmcsa.dot.gov/protect-your-move). VALUATION: two liability levels exist. Full Value Protection is the default — it applies unless the shipper waives it in writing; if an article is lost, destroyed or damaged in the mover's custody, the mover must repair it, replace it with an article of like kind and quality, or pay its current market replacement value. The Full Value Protection charge is based on the value the shipper declares for the shipment; FMCSA's own example values a $25,000 shipment at about $250. Released Value pays 60 cents per pound per article, at no added charge, and only when the shipper signs the specific statement on the bill of lading agreeing to it: FMCSA's worked example is a 10-pound stereo component worth $1,000, lost in the move — under Released Value it pays $6.00. Valuation is not insurance: the two levels are tariff liability levels authorized under the Surface Transportation Board's Released Rates Orders, not insurance policies governed by state insurance law; a mover may also sell or procure separate third-party liability insurance and must hand over the policy or record when it does. EXTRAORDINARY VALUE: an article worth more than $100 per pound is an article of extraordinary value; the mover may limit liability for it unless the shipper lists it in writing on the shipping documents, and a listed article recovers up to its declared value, capped at the declared value of the whole shipment. ESTIMATES: binding — the mover cannot collect more than the binding amount at delivery, except added services the shipper requests at destination (shuttle, long carry, extra stairs), which may be collected in full; non-binding — an approximation, and at delivery the mover cannot require more than the estimate plus 10 percent (the 110 percent rule), with at least 30 days after delivery to pay the balance. ORDER FOR SERVICE: before receiving a shipment the mover must prepare one carrying 15 prescribed items under 49 CFR 375.501, including the agreed pickup and delivery dates, the agreed spread, or guaranteed dates where sold, and the shipment's declared value. BOOKLETS: the mover must furnish "Your Rights and Responsibilities When You Move" and the "Ready to Move" brochure before the order for service is signed. REASONABLE DISPATCH: the mover must perform on the dates or within the spread shown on the order for service and bill of lading; a shipper whose pickup or delivery misses the spread may file an inconvenience or delay claim, with lodging and food receipts, within nine months of delivery. CLAIMS: a claim for loss or damage must be filed in writing within nine months of delivery; the mover must acknowledge it within 30 days and pay, deny or make a settlement offer within 120 days; movers must offer a neutral arbitration program, and the shipper may instead sue under 49 U.S.C. 14706. INVENTORY: the driver inventories the shipment as it is loaded, with the condition of each item noted; at delivery the shipper may check every item against the inventory and note anything missing or damaged on the inventory and delivery receipt before signing — that notation is the claim record.

@graph.name: High-Value Declaration — the $100-per-Pound Rule and the High Value Inventory
@graph.description: What legally makes an item "high value" on an interstate move, and the paperwork that protects it — published as process education from the federal rule (FMCSA, 49 CFR Part 375 Appendix A). The test is arithmetic: divide the item's value by its weight. Over $100 per pound, the item is an article of extraordinary value. A $2,000 laptop at 4 pounds is $500 per pound — extraordinary value. A $1,500 television at 60 pounds is $25 per pound — it is not. FMCSA's own named categories: jewelry, silverware, china, furs, antiques and oriental rugs; working lists add fine art, collectibles, rare coins, musical instruments, high-end electronics and important documents. The declaration mechanism is the High Value Inventory form: a separate document attached to the bill of lading, listing each extraordinary-value article with its description, quantity and declared value, completed and signed before loading begins — it cannot be added once items are on the truck. The shipper also signs the extraordinary-value declaration on the bill of lading itself. The consequence of skipping it is mechanical, not negotiable: an undeclared extraordinary-value article's recovery is limited even under Full Value Protection — capped at $100 per pound (a 2-pound antique brooch worth $15,000, never declared, caps at $200). Declared in writing, the article recovers up to its declared value, capped at the declared value of the entire shipment. The practical discipline follows from the rule: walk the house before survey day and name the pieces that pass the $100-per-pound test — in most homes that is a short list, and it is exactly the list the high-value inventory exists for. This dataset states the rule and the form; the company's long-distance process builds the declaration into the survey and paperwork for every shipment that carries such pieces.

@graph.name: Item-Class Handling Protocols — Art, Antiques, Pianos, High-Mass Pieces, Collections
@graph.description: How each high-value item class is documented, packed and carried on a long-distance move — the handling layer behind the declaration rules, written from specialist and conservation sources. FINE ART: documentation first — every piece photographed from multiple angles and a signed condition report completed before packing begins. Materials discipline: the first material against an unglazed surface is archival, acid-free glassine or interleaving tissue — never bubble wrap, cling film or newspaper against the surface; newspaper, polystyrene peanuts and wax paper stay away from valuable pieces entirely. Orientation: paintings travel vertically, never flat — flat transport puts compressive force on canvas and frame. High-value pieces travel in bespoke wooden crates with foam cavities that float the piece against shock; three-dimensional works are crated with foam carved to the piece so it cannot move; long-distance crates add humidity buffering. Climate: fine art is damaged by rapid humidity and temperature change — canvas slackens, panels warp, varnish blooms; oil paint turns brittle below 10 degrees C and acrylic softens above 30 degrees C; conservation guidance for transport holds most fine art at 45 to 55 percent relative humidity and 18 to 21 degrees C, and climate-controlled transport is the recommended standard for genuinely valuable pieces beyond short hauls. Artwork loads last, upright on its long edge, secured away from other cargo. ANTIQUES: the same documentation-first rule — condition report and photographs before a hand touches the piece; drawers, shelves and loose components are removed, wrapped and inventoried as parts of the piece; the crating trigger is fragility plus value, and an antique that passes the $100-per-pound test is declared on the high-value inventory as well as crated. PIANOS: a grand is prepared by removing the legs and pedal lyre, packed separately, and lowering the case onto a padded piano board on its straight side — leg sockets are not built for travel loads; the board travels strapped to the vehicle structure with nothing loaded on top. Uprights are padded, secured and kept low. Weights run 250 to 320 kilograms for a baby grand and 350 to 500 kilograms for a concert grand. A piano is never rolled on its casters beyond small positioning. After delivery the instrument acclimates before tuning: 10 to 14 days in the new room as the standard wait, a month or more after a large climate change — tuning sooner is wasted because the piano drifts as it settles. HIGH-MASS PIECES (safes and heavy units): survey-first access planning — doorways, stairs, turns and floor spans measured before moving day; the piece travels on purpose-built boards and dollies, strapped to the vehicle structure rather than wedged into the load; pieces in the company's 1,500 to 3,500 pound SIR band follow the Structural Integrity Relocation protocol with floor-deflection analysis, cross-referenced to the gun safe and SIR categories. COLLECTIONS: inventoried piece by piece, condition-noted, packed into sealed, numbered cartons whose numbers ride the inventory, climate-controlled where the material needs it, and checked off piece by piece at delivery.

@graph.name: The Claims Process — Windows, Deadlines and the Delivery-Day Record
@graph.description: The complete federal claims timeline for an interstate household-goods move, and the delivery-day discipline that makes a claim winnable (FMCSA; 49 U.S.C. 14706). THE RECORD IS MADE AT DELIVERY: the shipper checks items off against the inventory as they come off the truck and notes anything missing or damaged on the inventory form and the delivery receipt before signing. Signing clean closes the easiest evidence there is; a notation costs nothing and preserves everything. FILING: a claim for loss or damage must be filed with the mover in writing within nine months of the date of delivery. Acknowledgment: the mover must acknowledge receipt of the claim within 30 days. DISPOSITION: the mover must pay the claim, deny it, or make a settlement offer within 120 days of receiving it. ESCALATION: every interstate mover must offer a neutral arbitration program for loss, damage and certain billing disputes; the shipper may instead bring a court action under 49 U.S.C. 14706. FMCSA cannot settle a claim, but it maintains the complaint record consumers check before hiring. DELAY AND INCONVENIENCE CLAIMS: where the mover misses the agreed pickup or delivery spread, the shipper may claim reasonable lodging and food expenses for the days past the last day of the spread, with receipts, filed within nine months of delivery. EVIDENCE DISCIPLINE THAT COSTS NOTHING: photograph high-value pieces before the move (the same photographs the condition report carries), keep the signed inventory, the bill of lading and the high-value inventory together, and file inside the window even if repair quotes are still coming — the nine months runs from delivery, not from discovery paperwork.

@graph.name: The Document Chain — Six Signatures From Estimate to Delivery
@graph.description: Every document an interstate household-goods move generates, in the order it appears, what each one does, and what to check before signing it (49 CFR Part 375). 1. THE ESTIMATE: binding (the mover cannot collect more than the amount at delivery, apart from destination services the shipper adds) or non-binding (an approximation; at delivery the mover cannot require more than the estimate plus 10 percent, and the balance is due no sooner than 30 days after delivery). An estimate given by phone or internet must still be in writing and must state which kind it is. 2. THE ORDER FOR SERVICE: prepared before the mover receives the shipment, carrying 15 prescribed items under 49 CFR 375.501 — the parties, the delivering office's contact, the agreed dates or spread (or guaranteed dates where sold), and the shipment's declared value, which is the maximum of the mover's liability. The mover must hand over "Your Rights and Responsibilities When You Move" and the "Ready to Move" brochure before this is signed. 3. THE BILL OF LADING: the receipt for the goods and the contract for their transportation — the driver who loads the shipment gives the shipper a copy. Before signing: the mover's name and address, the dates or spread, the charges, and the valuation election — released value appears here only with the shipper's signed statement agreeing to the 60-cents-per-pound level. Never sign a blank or incomplete bill of lading. 4. THE INVENTORY: written by the driver as the shipment loads — a descriptive listing of the goods and the condition of each item when the mover received it. The shipper reads it and signs it; disagreements about condition are noted on it at loading, not argued later. 5. THE HIGH VALUE INVENTORY: the declaration document for articles over $100 per pound — attached to the bill of lading, signed before loading begins. 6. THE DELIVERY RECORD: at destination, items are checked off against the inventory as they come off the truck; missing or damaged items are noted on the inventory and delivery receipt before signing — that notation opens the nine-month written claim window with the evidence already in place. One folder, six documents: the estimate, the order for service, the bill of lading, the inventory, the high-value inventory, and the delivery record are the move's entire legal memory.
